name: Programming fundamentals vocabulary
description: The 100 terms every software developer needs: programming basics, data structures, design, debugging, git and concurrency.

cards.subject: variable
says: is a named place in a program that holds a value
can change its value as the program runs
cards.use: need to store a value and refer to it by name
not: is a value that can never change once it is set

cards.subject: constant
says: is a named value that does not change once it is set
is used for fixed values such as a tax rate or a limit
cards.use: need a named value that must not be changed by accident
not: is a value that changes every time the program runs

cards.subject: data type
says: describes what kind of value something is, such as a number or text
decides which operations are allowed on it
cards.use: need to say whether a value is a number, text or something else
not: is the name given to a variable

cards.subject: function
says: is a named block of code that does one job and can be used again
can take inputs and give back a result
cards.use: need to reuse the same steps in many places
not: is a single line that stores a value

cards.subject: parameter
says: is a named input that a function expects to receive
takes the value that the caller passes in
cards.use: need a function to work on whatever value it is given
not: is the value a function sends back

cards.subject: return value
says: is the result a function hands back to the code that called it
ends the function's work for that call
cards.use: need a function to give an answer to the caller
not: is an input passed in when the function is called

cards.subject: scope
says: is the part of a program in which a name can be used
limits where a variable can be read or changed
cards.use: find that a variable cannot be seen outside the function that made it
not: is the amount of work in a project

cards.subject: loop
says: repeats a block of code while a condition holds or for each item
saves writing the same steps many times
cards.use: need to do the same thing for every item in a list
not: runs a block of code exactly once

cards.subject: conditional
says: runs a block of code only when a condition is true
lets a program take different paths
cards.use: need a program to do one thing if a test passes and another if it does not
not: repeats code until the program ends

cards.subject: expression
says: is a piece of code that works out to a single value
can combine values, variables and operators
cards.use: need to name a piece of code such as 2 plus 3 that produces a value
not: is a complete instruction that always changes something

cards.subject: string
says: is a sequence of characters used for text
is usually written between quotation marks
cards.use: need to store a name or a sentence
not: is a whole number

cards.subject: integer
says: is a whole number with no fractional part
can be positive, negative or zero
cards.use: need to count items
not: is a number that can hold decimals

cards.subject: floating-point number
says: is a number that can have a fractional part
can be slightly inexact because of how computers store it
cards.use: need to store a measurement such as 3.14
not: is always exact for every decimal fraction

cards.subject: boolean
says: is a value that is either true or false
is the result of a comparison
cards.use: need to record whether something is on or off
not: is a value that can be any whole number

cards.subject: null
says: is a value that stands for no value
can cause errors if code assumes something is there
cards.use: need to show that a value is missing
not: is the number zero

cards.subject: array
says: is an ordered list of values reached by their position
usually starts counting positions from zero
cards.use: need to keep many values in order
not: is a collection of values reached by a name rather than a position

cards.subject: object
says: groups related data and the behaviour that works on it
is made from a class or written out directly
cards.use: need to model one thing, such as a customer, with its data
not: is a single number

cards.subject: dictionary
says: stores values that are looked up by a key
lets you find an entry without searching through all of them
cards.use: need to look up a value by name, such as a price by product
not: keeps values in a fixed order reached by position

cards.subject: set
says: is a collection of values with no duplicates
answers the question of whether a value is in it quickly
cards.use: need a collection in which each value appears once
not: is an ordered list that allows repeats

cards.subject: enumeration
says: is a type with a fixed list of named values
stops a variable taking a value that was never intended
cards.use: need a value that can only be one of a few named options
not: is a counter that goes up by one each time

cards.subject: recursion
says: is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the problem
needs a stopping case to end
cards.use: need to solve a problem that is made of smaller copies of itself
not: is repeating a block with a loop counter

cards.subject: exception
says: is an error condition that interrupts normal flow
can be caught and handled by code written for it
cards.use: need to deal with something going wrong, such as a missing file
not: is a rule that has no exceptions

cards.subject: callback
says: is a function passed to other code to be called later
lets code react when something finishes
cards.use: need code to run once a slow task completes
not: is the value returned when a function ends

cards.subject: promise
says: stands for a result that will be available later
can succeed with a value or fail with an error
cards.use: need to represent the eventual result of an asynchronous task
not: is a function that is called straight away

cards.subject: asynchronous code
says: starts a task and carries on without waiting for it to finish
handles the result when it arrives
cards.use: need the program to keep working while it waits for a slow request
not: runs each step to completion before starting the next

cards.subject: closure
says: is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created
keeps them available after that scope has ended
cards.use: need a function to keep access to values from its surroundings
not: is a function that closes a file

cards.subject: higher-order function
says: takes a function as input, returns one, or both
lets behaviour be passed around like data
cards.use: need to pass the rule for a task into a general-purpose function
not: is a function that runs faster than others

cards.subject: event loop
says: is the mechanism that picks up waiting tasks and runs them one at a time
lets a single-threaded program handle many asynchronous events
cards.use: need to explain how a program handles events without blocking
not: is a loop that runs the same code forever on every machine

cards.subject: side effect
says: is a change a function makes beyond returning a value
includes writing to a file or changing a variable outside it
cards.use: find that calling a function changes something outside itself
not: is the value a function returns

cards.subject: pure function
says: gives the same result for the same inputs
has no side effects
cards.use: want a function that is easy to test and reason about
not: changes shared state each time it runs

cards.subject: Big O notation
says: describes how the work of an algorithm grows as its input grows
ignores constant factors to show the overall trend
cards.use: need to compare how two approaches scale with more data
not: measures the exact running time in seconds

cards.subject: time complexity
says: is how the number of steps an algorithm takes grows with the size of its input
is usually written in Big O notation
cards.use: need to know how slow an approach will become with more data
not: is how much memory an algorithm uses

cards.subject: space complexity
says: is how the memory an algorithm uses grows with the size of its input
includes extra data it creates while it runs
cards.use: need to know whether an approach will run out of memory
not: is how long an algorithm takes to run

cards.subject: binary search
says: finds a value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the part to search
is far faster than checking each item in turn
cards.use: need to find a value quickly in a sorted list
not: works on a list in any order

cards.subject: sorting algorithm
says: puts items into a defined order
differs from others in speed, memory use and stability
cards.use: need items arranged in order, such as by date
not: finds a single item in a collection

cards.subject: divide and conquer
says: splits a problem into smaller parts, solves each and combines the results
underlies merge sort and binary search
cards.use: need to solve a big problem by breaking it into smaller ones
not: tries every possible answer in turn

cards.subject: dynamic programming
says: solves a problem by combining answers to overlapping smaller problems
stores each answer so that it is worked out only once
cards.use: see the same sub-problems being calculated again and again
not: is programming that changes itself while it runs

cards.subject: greedy algorithm
says: makes the best-looking choice at each step
does not always give the best overall answer
cards.use: need a quick approach that picks the best option available at every step
not: always finds the best overall answer

cards.subject: brute force
says: tries every possible answer until one works
is simple but becomes very slow as the problem grows
cards.use: need the simplest approach that is guaranteed to find an answer on a small problem
not: uses clever shortcuts to avoid checking most answers

cards.subject: memoisation
says: stores the result of a function call so that it is not calculated again
trades memory for speed
cards.use: need to avoid repeating an expensive calculation with the same input
not: deletes a function's result after it is used

cards.subject: linked list
says: is a chain of items, each pointing to the next
makes adding or removing in the middle cheap but reaching an item slow
cards.use: need to insert items often without moving the others
not: stores items side by side so that any one can be reached instantly

cards.subject: stack
says: adds and removes items only at one end
gives back the most recently added item first
cards.use: need last-in, first-out behaviour such as undo
not: gives back the oldest item first

cards.subject: queue
says: adds items at one end and removes them from the other
gives back the oldest item first
cards.use: need first-in, first-out behaviour such as a line of jobs
not: gives back the most recently added item first

cards.subject: binary tree
says: is a structure in which each item has at most two children
is the basis of many searching structures
cards.use: need a branching structure with at most two paths from each item
not: is a list in which each item has one successor

cards.subject: binary search tree
says: is a binary tree in which smaller values go left and larger go right
allows fast searching when it stays balanced
cards.use: need ordered data that supports quick lookup and insertion
not: is a tree in which values are stored in no particular order

cards.subject: graph
says: is a set of points joined by connections
models networks such as roads or friendships
cards.use: need to model things and the links between them
not: is a chart that plots numbers on two axes

cards.subject: heap
says: is a tree-shaped structure that keeps the smallest or largest item at the top
allows the top item to be removed quickly
cards.use: need to repeatedly take out the smallest or largest item
not: is the memory where a program's functions run

cards.subject: hash table
says: stores values by turning each key into a position
finds an entry in roughly constant time on average
cards.use: need very fast lookup by key
not: keeps its entries sorted by key

cards.subject: trie
says: is a tree that stores words by their shared prefixes
makes prefix searches, such as autocomplete, quick
cards.use: need to find all words that start with a given prefix
not: is a tree that stores numbers in sorted order

cards.subject: priority queue
says: gives back the item with the highest priority first, not the oldest
is often built on a heap
cards.use: need to process the most urgent job first
not: gives back items strictly in the order they arrived

cards.subject: class
says: is a blueprint for creating objects with shared data and behaviour
defines what its objects know and can do
cards.use: need a template for many similar objects
not: is one specific object in memory

cards.subject: inheritance
says: lets one class take on the data and behaviour of another
supports reuse by sharing what is common
cards.use: need a specialised class that builds on a general one
not: hides the inner workings of a class

cards.subject: polymorphism
says: lets different types respond to the same call in their own way
allows code to work with a general type
cards.use: need code to treat different kinds of object through the same interface
not: means a class can only ever take one form

cards.subject: encapsulation
says: keeps an object's data and the code that works on it together
hides the inner details behind a controlled interface
cards.use: need to stop other code changing an object's data directly
not: copies one object's data into another

cards.subject: abstraction
says: shows only what is needed and hides the detail
lets people use something without knowing how it works inside
cards.use: need to present a simple view of something complicated
not: keeps data and code together in one place

cards.subject: interface
says: defines what something can do without saying how
lets different implementations be used in the same way
cards.use: need several types to be used interchangeably
not: is the screen that a user sees

cards.subject: composition
says: builds a larger object from smaller ones it holds
is often preferred to inheritance for flexibility
cards.use: need an object to be made by combining other objects
not: makes one class a special case of another

cards.subject: constructor
says: is the code that sets up a new object when it is created
can take values that give the object its starting state
cards.use: need to set up an object's starting values as it is made
not: is the code that deletes an object

cards.subject: abstract class
says: is a class that cannot be used directly and is meant to be extended
may supply some behaviour and leave the rest to subclasses
cards.use: need a shared base that is never created on its own
not: is a class with no methods at all

cards.subject: dependency injection
says: gives an object the things it depends on instead of letting it create them
makes code easier to test and change
cards.use: need to swap a real service for a fake one in a test
not: makes an object create all its own dependencies

cards.subject: code smell
says: is a sign in the code that something may be wrong with the design
does not itself stop the program working
cards.use: see a function that has grown huge and does many things
not: is a bug that crashes the program

cards.subject: DRY principle
says: says that each piece of knowledge should live in one place
reduces the risk of changing one copy and forgetting another
cards.use: see the same logic copied in several places
not: says to repeat code so that each part stands alone

cards.subject: KISS principle
says: says to keep a design as simple as it can be
favours the simplest solution that works
cards.use: are tempted to build something more complicated than the problem needs
not: says to add every feature that might be useful

cards.subject: YAGNI
says: says not to build something until it is actually needed
stands for you aren't going to need it
cards.use: are asked to add a feature just in case it is wanted later
not: says to build everything up front

cards.subject: single responsibility principle
says: says a unit of code should have one reason to change
keeps each class or function focused on one job
cards.use: see a class that handles several unrelated jobs
not: says a class may have as many responsibilities as it likes

cards.subject: open-closed principle
says: says code should be open to extension but closed to modification
lets behaviour grow without rewriting what already works
cards.use: want to add new behaviour without editing tested code
not: says code should be closed to any change at all

cards.subject: separation of concerns
says: splits a program into parts that each deal with a separate matter
stops one change from rippling through everything
cards.use: need to keep user interface code apart from business rules
not: puts all the code for a feature into one place

cards.subject: magic number
says: is an unexplained number written directly in code
is better replaced by a named constant
cards.use: see the number 86400 in code with no explanation
not: is a number that always gives the right answer

cards.subject: dead code
says: is code that can never run or whose result is never used
clutters the program and should be removed
cards.use: find a function that nothing calls
not: is code that is running too slowly

cards.subject: technical documentation
says: explains how a system works and how to use or change it
helps new people learn the code
cards.use: need to explain to the next developer how a system fits together
not: is a list of every bug that was ever fixed

cards.subject: debugger
says: is a tool that lets you run a program step by step and inspect its state
shows the values of variables as it goes
cards.use: need to see what a program is doing at a particular line
not: is a tool that writes the program for you

cards.subject: breakpoint
says: is a marker that pauses a program at a chosen line
lets you inspect variables at that moment
cards.use: want the program to stop at a particular line so that you can look around
not: is a point at which the program crashes for good

cards.subject: stack trace
says: lists the chain of calls that led to an error
shows where in the code the error happened
cards.use: need to find which call caused an error report
not: is a list of all the files in a project

cards.subject: log level
says: sets how serious a log message is, such as debug, warning or error
lets people choose how much detail to see
cards.use: need to show only warnings and errors in production
not: is the amount of memory used by the log file

cards.subject: reproduction steps
says: are the exact actions that make a bug happen
let someone else see the problem for themselves
cards.use: need to report a bug so that a colleague can see it
not: are the steps taken to fix a bug

cards.subject: bisecting
says: finds the change that introduced a bug by repeatedly halving the range of history
works by testing a version in the middle each time
cards.use: know that a bug appeared sometime in the last hundred commits
not: tests every commit one at a time from the start

cards.subject: print debugging
says: adds output statements to see what values a program has
is simple and needs no special tool
cards.use: need a quick look at a value without setting up a debugger
not: means printing out the source code to read it

cards.subject: profiler
says: measures where a program spends its time or memory
shows which parts are worth making faster
cards.use: need to find out why a program is slow
not: checks whether the code follows the style rules

cards.subject: memory profiler
says: measures how a program uses memory over time
helps find where memory is being kept and not released
cards.use: see a program's memory use rise and not fall
not: measures how long each function takes to run

cards.subject: heisenbug
says: is a bug that changes or disappears when you try to observe it
often depends on timing or on the debugger itself
cards.use: find a bug that stops happening as soon as you add logging
not: is a bug that always happens in the same place

cards.subject: staging area
says: is where changes are collected before they are committed
lets you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit
cards.use: want to commit only some of the changes you have made
not: is the remote server that holds the repository

cards.subject: HEAD
says: is a pointer to the commit you are currently working from
normally moves forward when you make a commit
cards.use: need to know which commit your working copy is based on
not: is the first commit ever made in the repository

cards.subject: stash
says: sets aside uncommitted changes so that you can come back to them
leaves the working copy clean
cards.use: need to switch branch without committing half-finished work
not: permanently deletes your changes

cards.subject: cherry-pick
says: copies the changes of a chosen commit onto the current branch
lets one fix be applied without merging a whole branch
cards.use: need one specific fix from another branch
not: merges all the commits of a branch

cards.subject: squash merge
says: combines all the commits of a branch into a single commit when merging
keeps the main branch history short
cards.use: want a feature branch's many small commits to appear as one
not: keeps every commit of the branch in the history

cards.subject: fast-forward
says: moves a branch pointer forward when the other side has no new commits
needs no merge commit
cards.use: merge a branch where main has not moved since the branch began
not: creates a new commit joining two diverged branches

cards.subject: fetch
says: downloads new commits from a remote without changing your working files
lets you look at changes before combining them
cards.use: want to see what others have pushed without merging it yet
not: downloads and immediately merges the new commits

cards.subject: upstream
says: is the remote branch that a local branch tracks
decides where pushes and pulls go by default
cards.use: need to know which remote branch yours is linked to
not: is the oldest branch in the repository

cards.subject: detached HEAD
says: is the state of working from a particular commit rather than a branch
means new commits belong to no branch unless you save them
cards.use: check out an old commit and start making changes
not: is a branch that has been deleted from the remote

cards.subject: force push
says: overwrites the history on a remote with your local history
can destroy other people's work if it is misused
cards.use: have rewritten commits and need the remote to match
not: is a safe way to share changes that never loses anything

cards.subject: thread
says: is a path of execution within a program
shares memory with the other threads of the same program
cards.use: need a program to do several things at once inside one process
not: is a separate program with its own memory

cards.subject: process
says: is a running program with its own memory
is isolated from other processes
cards.use: need to describe a running program that is separate from others
not: is one path of execution that shares memory with others

cards.subject: concurrency
says: is dealing with many tasks at once by overlapping them in time
does not need them to run at the same instant
cards.use: need a program to make progress on several tasks together
not: is running tasks at the same instant on separate processors

cards.subject: parallelism
says: is running several tasks at the same instant on separate processors
speeds up work that can be split up
cards.use: need to use several processor cores to finish a job faster
not: is switching quickly between tasks on one core

cards.subject: mutex
says: lets only one thread at a time use a shared resource
makes other threads wait until it is released
cards.use: need to stop two threads changing the same data at once
not: lets any number of threads use a resource at the same time

cards.subject: deadlock
says: is when threads wait for each other forever
happens when each holds something that the other needs
cards.use: see two threads stuck, each waiting for the other to let go
not: is a thread that finishes too quickly

cards.subject: thread safety
says: means code behaves correctly when several threads use it at once
needs care with shared data
cards.use: need code to work correctly when it is called from many threads
not: means code is protected against hackers

cards.subject: garbage collection
says: frees memory that a program no longer uses, automatically
saves the developer from releasing memory by hand
cards.use: need memory cleaned up without writing code to free it
not: deletes files from the disk

cards.subject: heap memory
says: is the area of memory used for data that lives beyond a single function call
is shared between the parts of a program
cards.use: need to explain where long-lived objects are stored
not: is the area that records the chain of function calls

cards.subject: call stack
says: records the chain of function calls that are in progress
adds a frame when a function is called and removes it when it returns
cards.use: need to understand where an error occurred in a chain of calls
not: is the area that holds long-lived objects

qa.q: A tax rate must not be changed by accident. What should it be stored in?
wrong: A variable that is reassigned each time
qa.why: A constant holds a value that does not change.

qa.q: You need to do the same thing for every item in a list. What do you use?
qa.why: A loop repeats code for each item.

qa.q: You need the same steps in many places in a program. What do you write?
wrong: A separate program for each place
qa.why: A function can be reused.

qa.q: Which value is a boolean?
qa.why: A boolean is true or false.

qa.q: How do you reach the first item of an array in most languages?
qa.why: Positions usually start at zero.

qa.q: You want a program to stop at a chosen line so you can look at its variables. What do you set?
qa.why: A breakpoint pauses the program.

qa.q: You report a bug. What makes it easiest for a colleague to see it?
qa.right: The exact steps that make it happen
wrong: A description of how annoyed you are
The date you first noticed it
qa.why: Reproduction steps let others see the problem.

qa.q: What is a class?
qa.why: A class defines what its objects know and do.

qa.q: You need a quick look at a value without setting up a debugger. What can you do?
qa.why: Print debugging is simple and needs no tool.

qa.q: Which describes how the work of an algorithm grows as its input grows?
qa.why: Big O shows the growth trend.

qa.q: What must be true of a list for binary search to work?
wrong: It must be a linked list
qa.why: Binary search halves a sorted range.

qa.q: You need to look up a product's price by its name. Which structure suits it?
qa.why: A dictionary looks values up by key.

qa.q: An undo feature reverses the most recent action first. Which structure fits?
qa.why: A stack gives back the last item added.

qa.q: Print jobs must be handled in the order they arrive. Which structure fits?
qa.why: A queue gives back the oldest item first.

qa.q: Why does adding 0.1 and 0.2 not give exactly 0.3 in many languages?
qa.right: Floating-point numbers are stored in binary and can be slightly inexact
wrong: The language has a bug in addition
qa.why: Some decimals cannot be stored exactly.

qa.q: The same discount logic is copied into five places. Which principle does this break?
qa.right: DRY: each piece of knowledge should live in one place
qa.why: Repeated logic risks changing one copy and missing another.

qa.q: An error report lists the chain of calls that led to it. What is this?
qa.why: A stack trace shows where the error happened.

qa.q: You want to commit only some of the changes you have made. What helps?
qa.why: The staging area lets you choose what goes into a commit.

qa.q: You must switch branch but have half-finished work. What can you do?
wrong: Commit them to the wrong branch
qa.why: A stash sets work aside.

qa.q: You see the number 86400 in code with no explanation. What is it?
qa.right: A magic number, better replaced by a named constant
qa.why: Unexplained numbers hide their meaning.

qa.q: A recursive function never ends. What is it missing?
qa.why: Recursion needs a case that ends it.

qa.q: A page freezes while it waits for a slow request. What approach avoids this?
qa.right: Asynchronous code that carries on while it waits
qa.why: Asynchronous code does not block.

qa.q: A loop inside another loop, both over n items, takes roughly how many steps?
qa.why: Nested loops multiply.

qa.q: You need very fast lookup by key on average. Which structure fits?
qa.why: A hash table finds an entry in roughly constant time.

qa.q: Different shapes each draw themselves when you call draw on a general shape. What is this?
qa.why: Different types respond to the same call in their own way.

qa.q: Which is often preferred to inheritance for flexibility?
qa.why: Building from smaller objects is more flexible.

qa.q: A class sends emails, saves to the database and draws the page. Which principle does this break?
qa.why: A unit of code should have one reason to change.

qa.q: A function has grown to hundreds of lines and does many things. What is this called?
qa.why: It is a sign of a design problem.

qa.q: You need one specific fix from another branch without merging the whole branch. What do you use?
qa.why: Cherry-pick copies a chosen commit.

qa.q: What is the difference between a thread and a process?
qa.right: A thread shares memory with others in the same program; a process has its own memory
wrong: A thread is bigger than a process
A process shares memory with every other process
qa.why: Threads live inside a process.

qa.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
qa.right: Concurrency overlaps tasks in time; parallelism runs them at the same instant on separate processors
qa.why: Concurrency does not need simultaneous execution.

qa.q: Memory is freed for you automatically when it is no longer used. What does this?
qa.why: Garbage collection frees unused memory.

qa.q: Calling a function changes a variable outside it. What is this called?
qa.why: It changes something beyond the returned value.

qa.q: Merge sort splits a list, sorts each half and combines them. Which approach is this?
qa.why: It breaks a problem into smaller parts.

qa.q: You need to find out why a program is slow. What do you use?
qa.why: A profiler shows where time goes.

qa.q: A naive calculation repeats the same sub-problems over and over. What fixes it?
qa.right: Memoisation: store each result and reuse it
qa.why: Storing results avoids repeating work.

qa.q: Picking the largest coin each time does not always give the fewest coins. What does this show?
qa.right: A greedy algorithm does not always give the best overall answer
qa.why: Locally best choices can miss the best overall result.

qa.q: Two threads each hold something the other needs and both wait forever. What is this?
qa.why: Each waits for the other to let go.

qa.q: You need to stop two threads changing the same data at once. What can you use?
qa.why: A mutex lets one thread at a time in.

qa.q: A function keeps access to variables from where it was created, even after that scope ended. What is it?
qa.why: A closure remembers its surroundings.

qa.q: You want to swap a real service for a fake one in a test. What technique helps?
qa.why: Giving an object its dependencies makes testing easier.

qa.q: A bug appeared somewhere in the last hundred commits. What finds the commit that caused it fastest?
wrong: Testing every commit from the start
qa.why: Bisecting halves the range each time.

qa.q: You check out an old commit and start making changes. What state are you in?
qa.why: You are working from a commit, not a branch.

qa.q: A function always gives the same result for the same inputs and changes nothing else. What is it?
qa.why: Pure functions have no side effects.

qa.q: The most urgent job must always be processed first. Which structure fits?
qa.why: A priority queue gives back the highest priority first.

qa.q: You want to add new behaviour without editing tested code. Which principle fits?
qa.why: Code open to extension but closed to modification.

qa.q: A program's memory use rises and never falls. What tool helps find why?
qa.why: It shows where memory is being held.

qa.q: A bug disappears whenever you add logging. What is it called?
qa.why: It changes when observed.

qa.q: You need to find all words that start with a given prefix, as in autocomplete. Which structure fits?
qa.why: A trie stores words by shared prefixes.

qa.q: A colleague has rewritten commits and wants to force push. What is the risk?
qa.right: It can overwrite other people's work on the remote
qa.why: Force pushing replaces remote history.

qa.q: A function passed to another function so that it can be called later is used to react when something finishes. What is it?
qa.why: A callback is called when a task completes.
